source_neutral.procedure: Reconstruct the relative and absolute chronology of an undated correspondence bundle at two levels: the bundle, whose creator, recipient, later holders and accession history are partially known; and each letter, envelope, enclosure, draft or copy, whose writing, posting and receipt dates are unknown. Register candidate dating traces within and outside the bundle, assess their event-specific bounds, relative links and independence, cross-check them against independent records, and construct supported partial orders and date intervals while retaining gaps, conflicts and alternatives. The packet does not establish which traces exist, whether accompanying envelopes belong to their letters, whether the bundle represents one correspondence or a later assembly, or whether its physical arrangement preserves an earlier order. Each question remains open until checked.
source_neutral.action: 1. Before moving anything, record the bundle as found: assign each item an identifier and record its physical position, attachments, folds and enclosures. Keep this arrangement record separate from proposed writing order. 2. Enter every candidate dating trace for each item in a register, classifying it as an internal reference, material feature, inter-letter reference, or custody/annotation record. Candidate traces include postmarks and postage, letterhead, paper and watermarks, handwriting, recipient dockets or endorsements, internal mentions of events, persons, addresses or weekday/date combinations, references between letters, accession and custody records, and independent event records or calendars. 3. Classify each trace as supporting a not-before bound, a not-after bound or a relative link, such as B answering or citing A. Record whether it dates writing, posting, receipt, docketing or accession. 4. Record each trace's origin and possible derivation from another trace, such as a docket copied from an envelope or a catalogue date copied from a docket. Count dependent traces as one. 5. Cross-check against independent external records, including event records, calendars for weekday/date combinations, and accession or custody records. 6. Assemble supported relative links into a partial order and bounds into an interval for each item. Explicitly mark as gaps items without usable traces and intervals without supported links. 7. Retain each alternative chronology where a trace permits multiple placements. 8. For contradictions, recheck transcription, item identification, envelope-to-letter association, the event dated by the trace, and record independence, in that order. Record persistent conflicts as unresolved without averaging or silently discarding them.
source_neutral.observables: Look for compatible independent bounds that overlap for an item and inter-letter links that form an order without cycles and agree with those bounds. Look for contradictions: non-overlapping intervals for an item, cycles such as A preceding B preceding A, or custody records locating the bundle incompatibly with an item's bounds. Identify items without traces, items bounded on just one side, and stretches of the sequence without supported connecting links. Shared wording, shared errors or identical dates across records can suggest copying and dependence. Compare physical arrangement with the order supported by traces and record divergences. These are prospective signals; the packet reports no observations of them for this bundle.
source_neutral.inferential_warrant: Compatible independent links support a bounded reconstruction reported in three tiers: established, for a relative position or date interval supported by at least two independent, mutually compatible traces; provisional, for support from a single trace or traces whose independence has not been shown; and unresolved, for conflicting or absent support. Relative chronology is justified as a partial order: supported links order connected items, while other items remain unordered relative to one another. Absolute chronology is justified as intervals stated through not-before/not-after bounds, supporting traces and the event dated. A specific date is justified where an independent trace fixes it and the connection between that trace and the item is itself supported. A custody or accession date can bound the bundle, with items present at accession written no later than accession, under the stated assumption that the contents then were those now present. It does not establish internal item order. Physical arrangement supplies a hypothesis to test against traces, rather than evidence of writing order. If alternatives survive, report the set of alternative chronologies with their gaps marked.
source_neutral.problem_decomposition: Distinguish the bundle's custody history from the creation and exchange histories of its individual items. Distinguish letters, envelopes, enclosures, drafts and copies, and check their associations. Within each item, distinguish writing, posting, receipt, docketing and accession as separate events that traces may date. Relate traces to items and events, identify dependencies among records, and connect items through supported precedence relations. Combine bounds within each item and relative links across items without conflating physical position with chronological position. Custody follows a bundle through successive holders; dating its multiple items concerns their creation and exchange, so custody links do not establish writing order. If the bundle was assembled from several correspondences, one chronology may not apply.
source_neutral.next_inquiry: For each gap or conflict, identify and seek the specific independent record that would resolve it, such as a counterpart letter held elsewhere, an event record or another dated reference document. Whenever a new record is obtained, repeat external cross-checking, construction of the partial order and intervals, retention of alternative chronologies, and contradiction checking in steps 5–8.
source_neutral.limits: Counterpart letters, envelopes and accession files may be lost or inaccessible, leaving permanent gaps. Unsigned letters, shared names, recurring events and reused addresses can cause traces to be assigned to the wrong person, event or year. Items may be forged, backdated, misdated by their writers or misdocketed by recipients or later custodians. Dockets, catalogue entries and accession notes may repeat one earlier guess; agreement among dependent records does not provide independent confirmation. An accompanying envelope may be misassociated. A postmark dates posting rather than writing. Paper, watermarks and letterhead provide at most a not-before bound because stock may be used much later. Handwriting comparison supports coarse placement. A missing surviving reply does not establish that no reply was written, and an interval without surviving letters does not establish that correspondence stopped. An apparently continuous sequence may contain misplaced or misidentified items or undocumented breaks. The procedure is a scoped authored hypothesis, not verified practitioner consensus, and does not rely on quantitative alignment of long measured sequences. Stop when every item has a cited interval and/or order position or is explicitly marked unplaced, and checking remaining accessible records no longer changes any bound or order relation, or when accessible records are exhausted.
